Space complexity. Space complexity measures the amount of memory or auxiliary storage an algorithm uses as a function of input size, expressed in Big O notation like O of one, O of log n, or O of n. While time complexity dominates practical concern, space complexity is critical for resource-constrained systems and for theoretical understanding of computational limits.

Space complexity measures the maximum amount of extra memory needed as a function of input size n. Constant space, O of one, means an algorithm uses a fixed amount of memory regardless of input size—like comparing two numbers. Logarithmic space, O of log n, is used by many divide-and-conquer algorithms and is more efficient than linear. Linear space, O of n, is proportional to input size and is used by many sorting and tree algorithms. Exponential space, O of two to the n, is infeasible for large inputs and appears in some exhaustive search and dynamic programming solutions.

PSPACE is the complexity class of problems solvable with polynomial space, though they may take exponential time. The proven relationships are P is a subset of NP is a subset of PSPACE. All three of these containments are proven. There's often a space-time tradeoff in algorithm design. You can reduce space by using more time—for instance, by recomputing values instead of storing them—or you can trade time for space by caching results. Savitch's theorem relates deterministic and nondeterministic space complexity. It says nondeterministic space is at most quadratically worse than deterministic space. Specifically, nondeterministic space of f of n is contained in deterministic space of f of n squared.
